content: An analysis of the intersection between rail infrastructure and coal logistics reveals that transport delays, infrastructure capacity, and overarching supply chain reliability are the primary mechanisms through which rail dynamics influence toll washing operations. Understanding these relationships requires a comprehensive evaluation of macro-level rail industry trends, regional network performance, and the specific logistical bottlenecks that arise within the coal supply chain. Infrastructure capacity fundamentally determines the maximum throughput and peak demand limits for toll washing facilities. When rail networks operate at or near optimal capacity, processing plants can maintain steady, predictable washing cycles. Recent macro-level data indicates significant movements within the broader United States rail sector, which indirectly shape the baseline capacity available for bulk commodities like coal. For instance, rail traffic data from January 2026 demonstrated a 9.7 percent increase in carloads and intermodal units compared to the prior year, reflecting a robust rising demand for rail transport services early in the year [81] . Furthermore, the broader rail supply industry continues to represent a massive economic force, supporting approximately 906,000 jobs across the nation [82] . To sustain and potentially expand this capacity, industry forecasts from early 2026 predict that annual railcar delivery levels will meet or exceed replacement needs by the 2027 to 2028 timeframe, ensuring that the physical rolling stock remains adequate for future industrial demands [83] . However, maintaining this infrastructure capacity is not without significant hurdles. By integrating real-time rail network intelligence into their operational planning, processing facilities can better anticipate delivery fluctuations, mitigate the impact of transport delays, and align their washing cycles with the prevailing realities of the coal supply chain.
